newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin health news a move to U.S.-style openness.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin health news a move to U.S.-style openness.

text.p: It wasn't so very long ago that health problems of U.S. presidents were closely guarded secrets. Nowadays, the public gets detailed medical bulletins -- polyps, cysts, prostates and all.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin's announcement that he will have heart surgery is a dramatic change for the Kremlin, which for decades sought to hide illnesses of Soviet leaders.

Secrecy is not unique to the Kremlin. The late French President Francois Mitterand was more open about his love life than his bone cancer, which he kept secret for 11 years. China-watchers around the world would dearly like to know more about the health of Beijing's gerontocracy.

Even Yeltsin's candor had limits. Much was left unsaid about the specifics of his case. How he fares, through bypass surgery and the subsequent rehabilitation, could depend in part on his overall health, whether he has prior damage to his heart muscle or valves, or problems with his liver or kidneys.

Yeltsin's statement, however, was a break with tradition, a step toward the hallmark American openness where the health of presidents, presidential candidates and presidential wives has become part of political discourse and a reflection of the diminishing private sphere left for those in public life.

"The relationship between the president and the public has become far more personal... Everything personal has become political, nothing is out of bounds," said American Enterprise Institute political analyst Bill Schneider, crediting the influence of television and the decline of political parties.

In an America coloured by tell-all talk shows and sensational public confessionals, it is now routine for voters to get personal accounts not just of life-threatening diseases like Ronald Reagan's colon cancer, but less serious ailments.
They've heard about Jimmy Carter's haemorrhoids, Reagan's enlarged prostate, George and Barbara Bush's thyroid woes, and President's Clinton's ingrown pimple.

"The right to privacy has significantly eroded. And it isn't just about medical matters. It's also about personal relationships," said Dr. Jerald Post, a George Washington University psychiatrist who is the co-author of a book called "When Illness Strikes the Leader".
In the 19th century, President Grover Cleveland had two malignant growths removed in a secret operation held on a boat in the Hudson River, historians have learned.
Woodrow Wilson's White House kept his devastating 1919 stroke a secret for four months.
Everyone knew Franklin Roosevelt had polio. But few knew that he was so crippled that he was often in a wheelchair.
It's hard to pinpoint when the norms changed, although some date it to Dwight Eisenhower's 1955 heart attack.

"Eisenhower's illness was fairly well known and we got reports from the hospital, pulse rate and bowel movements -- more information I think than most people wanted," said Stephen Wayne, a Georgetown political scientist.

Eisenhower's successor John Kennedy, so celebrated for his youth and vigour, covered up his Addison's Disease, according to biographers. It was his death, from a bullet not a disease, that contributed to the public's growing concern with the president's health, said Wayne.
"After Kennedy's assassination," he said, "we got more concerned about filling offices like the vice presidency."
